chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Isa ibn Ubayd, from Ja'far ibn Isa who said:

I wrote to Abu Al-Hasan (peace be upon him) asking him regarding a man who bequeathed some of his one-third from after his death, from the yield of his estate, to an executor to place half of it in known places he had mentioned to him during every year, and the remainder of the one-third he can act regarding it with whatever he so desires and the executor agrees with it. So the executor enforced what had been bequeathed to him from the known named, and said regarding the remainder, 'I have rendered for so and so such and such (amount), and for so and so such and such (amount), in every year, and regarding the Hajj, such and such (amount), and regarding the charity such and such (amount) during every year. Then he changed with regards to all of that', so he said, 'I have decided that the first of what I view as being opposite of my first desires and views'. Is it for him that he retracts with regards to it, and give what he gives to others, or reduces them, or includes other along with them, if he so wants that?' So he (peace be upon him) wrote: 'It is for him that he does whatever he so desires to, except if there happens to be a written agreement upon himself'.
ai.seo_question: Can a testator change the distribution of the one-third bequest after the executor has already allocated it?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the principle of *khiyar* (optionality) in the execution of wills, specifically addressing the testator's right to revoke or modify the discretionary distribution of the remaining one-third of the estate after the executor has acted. Imam al-Rida (AS) clarifies that such changes are permissible unless the testator had previously bound himself through a formal written contract (*kitaban ala nafsihi*), highlighting the distinction between unilateral testamentary freedom and binding contractual obligations in Shia jurisprudence. This ruling underscores the flexibility granted to the testator in managing his posthumous wealth, provided no irrevocable legal commitment was made.
